screens.title: Interfaces and Default Methods
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you will learn what interfaces are in Java, why they matter for designing flexible systems, and how Java 8 extended them with default and static methods. An interface is a contract: it names behaviors a class must provide without imposing state or a specific implementation. This allows unrelated classes to share capabilities and be used polymorphically when they implement the same interface. You will see concrete examples like Flyable, where both Bird and Airplane implement the same behavior in their own way. We will also explore how default methods let library authors add new behavior without breaking existing implementations, and how static methods provide utility functions grouped with the interface. Along the way we will contrast interfaces with abstract classes, highlight common mistakes such as attempting to add instance fields to an interface, and practice a hands-on example where devices implement a shared ElectronicDevice interface and selectively override a default reset. By the end of the chapter you'll understand how interfaces support multiple inheritance of type, how default and static methods change evolution strategies for APIs, and practical guidelines for choosing interfaces versus abstract classes.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.narratorSegment: By the end of this chapter you will be able to define what an interface is in Java and explain its role as a behavioral contract. You will compare interfaces with abstract classes and articulate the key differences that affect inheritance, fields, and constructors. You will implement interfaces to leverage multiple inheritance of type, enabling a single class to conform to several contracts and to be used polymorphically. Finally, you will use Java 8 features: add default methods to interfaces when evolving APIs and call static methods on interfaces for utility behavior. Each objective emphasizes practical use: knowing when to choose an interface improves system modularity and testing, understanding default methods prevents breakage when libraries evolve, and knowing static methods helps organize utilities. These skills are essential when designing loosely coupled components and when maintaining public APIs. You'll practice these skills with examples such as Flyable and ElectronicDevice, and you'll complete a small coding exercise that uses a default method and an override to see the compatibility behavior firsthand.

screens.title: What is an Interface?
screens.narratorSegment: An interface in Java is a declared contract that lists method signatures and constants a class that implements it must provide. It focuses on behavior — what methods exist — and intentionally avoids specifying how those behaviors are implemented or storing instance state. In early Java versions interfaces contained only abstract method signatures and public static final constants, so they were used purely to express capabilities. This makes interfaces excellent for defining capabilities shared across unrelated classes: for example, Flyable declares fly and land, and both Bird and Airplane implement those methods in their own way. Because interfaces define type, a variable declared with an interface type can reference any object that implements the interface, enabling polymorphism and loose coupling. A common misconception is to treat an interface as a place for shared data; interfaces are not for instance variables. Another confusion is mixing up implements and extends: classes implement interfaces and extend classes. Knowing this distinction helps you design cleaner APIs that describe behavior separately from object state. Think of an interface as a signed agreement: it promises certain actions without dictating internal structure or storage.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › What is an Interface?
Core definition

An interface declares method signatures and constants; implementing classes provide concrete behavior. Interfaces express capability and type, not state.

Analogy
A signed agreement lists required actions but not how to perform them. Different signers fulfill the same promises in their own way.
Common misconception
Interfaces are not for instance variables. They do not hold per-object state; they describe behavior only.
Concrete example
// Interface definition
interface Flyable {
  void fly(); // implicitly public abstract
  void land();
}

// Two unrelated classes implement Flyable and provide their own behavior
Key Takeaway

Use interfaces to define capabilities and enable polymorphism across unrelated types.

screens.title: Implementing an Interface: Flyable Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through a concrete implementation of an interface to see polymorphism in action. The Flyable interface declares two methods: fly and land. A Bird implements Flyable by providing an implementation that describes flapping wings and gentle landing. An Airplane implements the same interface but with engine-powered flight and runway landing. At runtime you can declare a variable of type Flyable and assign either a Bird or an Airplane. Calling fly on that variable invokes the appropriate implementation for the actual object — this is polymorphism: the code uses the interface type and remains decoupled from concrete classes. A common misconception is that interfaces limit what code can do; in fact they increase flexibility because code written to an interface can accept new implementations without modification. This example also shows why interfaces model behavior: Bird and Airplane do not need a shared superclass to be used polymorphically; they only need to fulfill the same contract. After you study the code, consider how adding a new default method would affect existing classes — they remain compatible unless you introduce an abstract method.

keyIdea.title: Polymorphism

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Flyable Walkthrough
Code example
interface Flyable {
  void fly();
  void land();
}

class Bird implements Flyable {
  @Override
  public void fly() {
    System.out.println("Bird is flapping its wings and flying.");
  }
  @Override
  public void land() {
    System.out.println("Bird is landing gently on a branch.");
  }
}

class Airplane implements Flyable {
  @Override
  public void fly() {
    System.out.println("Airplane is soaring through the sky with engines roaring.");
  }
  @Override
  public void land() {
    System.out.println("Airplane is landing on a runway.");
  }
}

public class AirTrafficControl {
  public static void main(String[] args) {
    Flyable myBird = new Bird();
    Flyable myPlane = new Airplane();

    myBird.fly();
    myPlane.fly();
  }
}
Explanation & example
  • Flyable declares behavior; Bird and Airplane provide their own implementations for fly and land.
  • Variables typed as Flyable can reference any implementer, enabling polymorphic calls.
  • This decouples code from concrete classes; new implementers can be added without changing callers.
Analogy
Think of Flyable as a pilot license: many vehicles or animals can hold the license and fly differently, but all promise the same basic skills.
Key Takeaway

Use interfaces to write code against behavior, not implementation, so your systems remain extensible.

screens.title: Interfaces vs Abstract Classes
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing between an interface and an abstract class depends on whether you need to share behavior only or also share state and partial implementations. Interfaces define contracts without instance state; they allow a class to implement many interfaces and thus achieve multiple inheritance of type. Abstract classes can hold instance fields, provide constructors, and include concrete methods that share implementation among subclasses, but a class can extend only one abstract class. Before Java 8 interfaces were purely abstract, but since Java 8 they can include default, static, and private methods, which narrows the behavioral difference but does not change the inheritance of state. Use an interface when you want unrelated classes to promise the same behavior without imposing a shared data model. Use an abstract class when you have a family of related classes that should share state or common implementation. A common mistake is to try to force shared object state into an interface; instead use an abstract class or composition. Consider maintenance: interfaces are better for flexible APIs, abstract classes for template methods and shared fields. Interfaces vs Abstract Classes means interfaces = multiple behavioral contracts; abstract classes = shared state and partial implementation for related types.. In practical terms, key differences that affect design decisions. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Interfaces vs Abstract Classes
Side-by-side
Interface
  • Behavior only (method signatures)
  • Implement multiple interfaces
  • No instance constructors
  • Constants only for fields
  • Can have default/static methods (Java 8+)
Abstract Class
  • Can hold instance fields and constructors
  • Single inheritance (one superclass)
  • Can mix abstract and concrete methods
  • Useful to share implementation and state
Example scenario

If you need a common ID field and shared save behavior, an abstract class can hold the field and methods. If you need an ability like Serializable or Flyable across different, unrelated classes, use an interface.

Misconception check
Default methods mean interfaces are now the same as abstract classes. They are not: interfaces still cannot hold per-instance state or constructors.
Key Takeaway

Choose interfaces for shared capabilities and abstract classes for shared state or partial implementation across a related type hierarchy.

screens.title: Default Methods: Evolving Interfaces Safely
screens.narratorSegment: Default methods were introduced in Java 8 to allow interfaces to evolve — to add new behavior without requiring every implementing class to change. A default method includes a concrete implementation within the interface and is marked with the default keyword. Consider adding takeOff to Flyable as a default method that prints a preparation message. Existing classes like Bird and Airplane continue to compile because the default supplies an implementation. Implementers are free to override the default to provide specialized behavior, such as a Helicopter overriding takeOff to include rotor checks. A common mistake is to assume defaults replace abstract design; defaults are intended to aid evolution, not to provide extensive shared state or complex logic. If many classes need a sophisticated shared implementation that depends on state, prefer an abstract class or composition. Another subtlety: if a class implements two interfaces that provide conflicting defaults with the same signature, the class must resolve the conflict by overriding the method. Default methods therefore increase flexibility but also add a resolution step in multiple inheritance scenarios of type. Default Methods: Evolving Interfaces Safely means default methods let interfaces add concrete behavior to support api evolution while preserving backward compatibility.. In practical terms, how default methods let you add behavior without breaking implementers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Default Methods
Default method example
interface Flyable {
  void fly();
  void land();

  default void takeOff() {
    System.out.println("Preparing for takeoff.");
  }
}

class Helicopter implements Flyable {
  @Override
  public void fly() { System.out.println("Helicopter is hovering."); }
  @Override
  public void land() { System.out.println("Helicopter is landing vertically."); }
  // can use default takeOff() or override it
}
Why it matters
  • Default methods prevent breaking changes when adding methods to widely used interfaces.
  • Implementers may override defaults to provide specialized behavior.
  • If two interfaces provide a default with the same signature, the implementing class must disambiguate by overriding.
Pitfall
Do not use default methods to hide complex shared state requirements. Prefer an abstract class if shared state and constructors are needed.
Key Takeaway

Use default methods to evolve interfaces safely; override them when implementers need custom behavior.

screens.title: Static Methods in Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: Static methods in interfaces are utilities that logically belong with the interface, but they are not called on instances — they are invoked on the interface type itself. This is useful for helper functions related to the interface's purpose. For example, an interface named Converter could provide a static convertToInt method that all implementers can call to parse values in a consistent way. Static methods do not participate in polymorphism; they are not inherited by implementers for dispatching and cannot be overridden in the usual sense. A common confusion is attempting to call a static method on an implementing class instance — static methods must be called on the interface name. Static methods help organize code by grouping utilities with the contract they support, improving discoverability. Remember that static interface methods do not change an implementing object's behavior automatically; they are simply namespaced helper functions associated with the interface. Static Methods in Interfaces means static interface methods provide interface-scoped utilities and must be called on the interface, not on instances.. In practical terms, utility functions that belong to the interface itself. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Static Methods
Static utility example
interface Converter {
  int convert(String s);

  static int convertToInt(String s) {
    return Integer.parseInt(s.trim());
  }
}

// Usage:
// int n = Converter.convertToInt("42");
Notes
  • Static methods belong to the interface itself and are called on the interface name.
  • They are useful for utility logic closely tied to the interface's purpose.
  • They are not polymorphic and cannot be called through an instance reference.
Misuse to avoid
Avoid placing behavior that depends on instance state into static methods; those belong elsewhere.
Key Takeaway

Use static interface methods to group related utilities with the contract for discoverability and cohesion.

screens.title: Evolving an Interface with a Default Method
screens.narratorSegment: Evolving a public interface requires care to avoid breaking existing implementers. Java 8's default methods provide a way to add a new method with a default implementation so old classes continue to compile. The process is straightforward: add the new method to the interface and mark it default with a reasonable implementation. Existing classes inherit that implementation automatically and need no changes. New classes may override the default to provide specialized behavior. If your default relies on other abstract methods, ensure those methods will behave correctly for existing implementers. Also test the case where a class implements two interfaces that both offer a default with the same signature — the compiler will require the class to override and resolve the conflict. Practically, use default methods when you can provide a safe, general implementation during A P I evolution. If the method cannot have a sensible default for all implementers, consider creating a new interface or providing a utility class instead. This process keeps libraries usable by older code while allowing the A P I to grow responsibly. Evolving an Interface with a Default Method means add a default method to preserve backward compatibility; resolve conflicts explicitly when multiple defaults collide.. In practical terms, add a default method and observe compatibility with existing implementers. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › Evolving an Interface
Step-by-step
  1. Add the new method to the interface and mark it default with a safe implementation.
  2. Run compilation against existing implementations to verify compatibility.
  3. If conflicts arise from multiple defaults, require implementers to override and resolve.
  4. Consider tests and documentation showing intended default behavior.
Concrete example
// Add a new default method safely
interface Flyable {
  void fly();
  void land();
  default void takeOff() { System.out.println("Preparing for takeoff."); }
}

// Existing classes compile and use the default takeOff() automatically
Misconception
Default methods remove the need for careful design. They help evolution, but meaningful defaults must be safe for all implementers.

screens.title: Common Mistakes When Using Interfaces
screens.narratorSegment: There are several recurring mistakes developers make with interfaces. First, trying to place instance variables inside an interface is incorrect: interface fields are implicitly public static final constants and are not per-instance state. If you need per-instance data, use an abstract class or composition. Second, confusing implements with extends can lead to wrong assumptions about inheritance: classes implement interfaces and extend classes; extends implies single inheritance for classes. Third, relying on default methods for complex stateful behavior is risky; defaults should be simple, safe fallbacks. Fourth, when a class implements two interfaces that provide the same default method signature, you must explicitly override and select the appropriate implementation to avoid ambiguity. Finally, attempting to call an interface static method from an instance or expecting it to be polymorphic will cause confusion; static methods belong to the interface and are not dispatched dynamically. Following best practices: keep interfaces focused on behavior, keep default methods minimal and safe, prefer abstract classes or composition for shared state, and clearly resolve default conflicts in classes that implement multiple interfaces. Common Mistakes When Using Interfaces means do not store instance state in interfaces; use defaults sparingly; resolve default conflicts explicitly; call static methods on the interface name.. In practical terms, avoid errors with fields, constructors, and method resolution. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Module 3 › Chapter 3.2 › ElectronicDevice Activity
Starter code template
// 1. Define the ElectronicDevice interface
interface ElectronicDevice {
  void powerOn();
  void powerOff();

  default void reset() {
    System.out.println("Device is performing a soft reset.");
  }
}

// 2. Define Smartphone class implementing ElectronicDevice
class Smartphone implements ElectronicDevice {
  @Override
  public void powerOn() { System.out.println("Smartphone is booting up."); }
  @Override
  public void powerOff() { System.out.println("Smartphone is shutting down."); }
  // uses default reset()
}

// 3. Define Laptop class overriding reset()
class Laptop implements ElectronicDevice {
  @Override
  public void powerOn() { System.out.println("Laptop is starting Windows."); }
  @Override
  public void powerOff() { System.out.println("Laptop is entering sleep mode."); }
  @Override
  public void reset() { System.out.println("Laptop is performing a hard reboot."); }
}

// 4. Main to test behavior: create instances and call methods
Checklist
  • Interface includes default reset method.
  • Smartphone uses default reset without override.
  • Laptop overrides reset with a hard reboot message.
  • Main demonstrates both behaviors through instance calls.

This activity shows default methods preserve compatibility while letting implementers customize behavior.

screens.title: When to Use Interfaces in System Design
screens.narratorSegment: Interfaces are powerful tools for designing loosely coupled systems. Use them to define capabilities that many different, otherwise unrelated types can support — for example, serializable behavior, iterable behavior, or a Flyable capability. They are especially helpful when you want to program to an abstraction so that components can be swapped or mocked easily in tests. When deciding whether to create an interface, ask: will multiple unrelated classes need to share this behavior? If yes, an interface is a good fit. If you also need shared state, constructors, or partial implementation, favor an abstract class or composition. In A P I design, keep interfaces small and focused so implementers have minimal obligations; consider grouping related behaviors into several small interfaces rather than one large one. Use default methods for safe, general-purpose fallbacks, and static methods for utilities. In many cases composition combined with interfaces produces cleaner, testable code: define a small behavior interface and use composition to share implementation details. These practices support extensibility, easier testing, and clearer separation between behavior and state. When to Use Interfaces in System Design means prefer small, focused interfaces for behavior and use abstract classes or composition for shared state or implementation details.. screens.title: Multiple Inheritance of Type
screens.narratorSegment: Multiple inheritance of type is the ability of a single class to implement many interfaces and thereby conform to multiple contracts. This differs from multiple inheritance of implementation, which Java does not allow for classes. By implementing multiple interfaces a class promises to provide the behaviors declared by each interface, enabling it to play many roles. For instance, a class could implement Flyable and Trackable, allowing it to both fly and expose location updates. This composition of capabilities makes objects highly flexible and testable: code can depend on a narrow interface rather than a large monolithic type. However, when interfaces provide default methods, multiple inheritance of type can create conflicts if two interfaces provide the same default method signature; the implementing class must resolve the conflict by overriding. Use multiple interfaces to keep each contract focused and to mix and match capabilities as needed. A useful pattern is to design small interfaces for single responsibilities and compose them in classes that need multiple behaviors. This approach supports the single responsibility principle and keeps implementations easier to maintain and evolve. fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you will learn what interfaces are in Java, why they matter for designing flexible systems, and how Java 8 extended them with default and static methods. An interface is a contract: it names behaviors a class must provide without imposing state or a specific implementation. This allows unrelated classes to share capabilities and be used polymorphically when they implement the same interface. You will see concrete examples like Flyable, where both Bird and Airplane implement the same behavior in their own way. We will also explore how default methods let library authors add new behavior without breaking existing implementations, and how static methods provide utility functions grouped with the interface. Along the way we will contrast interfaces with abstract classes, highlight common mistakes such as attempting to add instance fields to an interface, and practice a hands-on example where devices implement a shared ElectronicDevice interface and selectively override a default reset. By the end of the chapter you'll understand how interfaces support multiple inheritance of type, how default and static methods change evolution strategies for APIs, and practical guidelines for choosing interfaces versus abstract classes.

By the end of this chapter you will be able to define what an interface is in Java and explain its role as a behavioral contract. You will compare interfaces with abstract classes and articulate the key differences that affect inheritance, fields, and constructors. You will implement interfaces to leverage multiple inheritance of type, enabling a single class to conform to several contracts and to be used polymorphically. Finally, you will use Java 8 features: add default methods to interfaces when evolving APIs and call static methods on interfaces for utility behavior. Each objective emphasizes practical use: knowing when to choose an interface improves system modularity and testing, understanding default methods prevents breakage when libraries evolve, and knowing static methods helps organize utilities. These skills are essential when designing loosely coupled components and when maintaining public APIs. You'll practice these skills with examples such as Flyable and ElectronicDevice, and you'll complete a small coding exercise that uses a default method and an override to see the compatibility behavior firsthand.

These objectives focus on demonstrable skills: implementing an interface across unrelated classes and using default methods so existing implementations remain stable. You will implement an example like Flyable and verify polymorphic calls work when different types implement the same contract. You will also write and call static methods on an interface to group utilities with the contract. The assessment checks your understanding of multiple inheritance of type — why a class can implement many interfaces but extend only one class — and tests your ability to spot common errors, such as trying to add instance fields to an interface or calling an interface static method from an instance. Practically, these abilities let you build cleaner APIs and maintain libraries with less breaking change. During practice you will override a default reset method on one implementation to see how behavior can differ across implementers, reinforcing when to accept a default and when to provide a specialized implementation.

An interface in Java is a declared contract that lists method signatures and constants a class that implements it must provide. It focuses on behavior — what methods exist — and intentionally avoids specifying how those behaviors are implemented or storing instance state. In early Java versions interfaces contained only abstract method signatures and public static final constants, so they were used purely to express capabilities. This makes interfaces excellent for defining capabilities shared across unrelated classes: for example, Flyable declares fly and land, and both Bird and Airplane implement those methods in their own way. Because interfaces define type, a variable declared with an interface type can reference any object that implements the interface, enabling polymorphism and loose coupling. A common misconception is to treat an interface as a place for shared data; interfaces are not for instance variables. Another confusion is mixing up implements and extends: classes implement interfaces and extend classes. Knowing this distinction helps you design cleaner APIs that describe behavior separately from object state. Think of an interface as a signed agreement: it promises certain actions without dictating internal structure or storage.

Let's walk through a concrete implementation of an interface to see polymorphism in action. The Flyable interface declares two methods: fly and land. A Bird implements Flyable by providing an implementation that describes flapping wings and gentle landing. An Airplane implements the same interface but with engine-powered flight and runway landing. At runtime you can declare a variable of type Flyable and assign either a Bird or an Airplane. Calling fly on that variable invokes the appropriate implementation for the actual object — this is polymorphism: the code uses the interface type and remains decoupled from concrete classes. A common misconception is that interfaces limit what code can do; in fact they increase flexibility because code written to an interface can accept new implementations without modification. This example also shows why interfaces model behavior: Bird and Airplane do not need a shared superclass to be used polymorphically; they only need to fulfill the same contract. After you study the code, consider how adding a new default method would affect existing classes — they remain compatible unless you introduce an abstract method.

Choosing between an interface and an abstract class depends on whether you need to share behavior only or also share state and partial implementations. Interfaces define contracts without instance state; they allow a class to implement many interfaces and thus achieve multiple inheritance of type. Abstract classes can hold instance fields, provide constructors, and include concrete methods that share implementation among subclasses, but a class can extend only one abstract class. Before Java 8 interfaces were purely abstract, but since Java 8 they can include default, static, and private methods, which narrows the behavioral difference but does not change the inheritance of state. Use an interface when you want unrelated classes to promise the same behavior without imposing a shared data model. Use an abstract class when you have a family of related classes that should share state or common implementation. A common mistake is to try to force shared object state into an interface; instead use an abstract class or composition. Consider maintenance: interfaces are better for flexible APIs, abstract classes for template methods and shared fields. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Default methods were introduced in Java 8 to allow interfaces to evolve — to add new behavior without requiring every implementing class to change. A default method includes a concrete implementation within the interface and is marked with the default keyword. Consider adding takeOff to Flyable as a default method that prints a preparation message. Existing classes like Bird and Airplane continue to compile because the default supplies an implementation. Implementers are free to override the default to provide specialized behavior, such as a Helicopter overriding takeOff to include rotor checks. A common mistake is to assume defaults replace abstract design; defaults are intended to aid evolution, not to provide extensive shared state or complex logic. If many classes need a sophisticated shared implementation that depends on state, prefer an abstract class or composition. Another subtlety: if a class implements two interfaces that provide conflicting defaults with the same signature, the class must resolve the conflict by overriding the method. Default methods therefore increase flexibility but also add a resolution step in multiple inheritance scenarios of type. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Static methods in interfaces are utilities that logically belong with the interface, but they are not called on instances — they are invoked on the interface type itself. This is useful for helper functions related to the interface's purpose. For example, an interface named Converter could provide a static convertToInt method that all implementers can call to parse values in a consistent way. Static methods do not participate in polymorphism; they are not inherited by implementers for dispatching and cannot be overridden in the usual sense. A common confusion is attempting to call a static method on an implementing class instance — static methods must be called on the interface name. Static methods help organize code by grouping utilities with the contract they support, improving discoverability. Remember that static interface methods do not change an implementing object's behavior automatically; they are simply namespaced helper functions associated with the interface. Evolving a public interface requires care to avoid breaking existing implementers. Java 8's default methods provide a way to add a new method with a default implementation so old classes continue to compile. The process is straightforward: add the new method to the interface and mark it default with a reasonable implementation. Existing classes inherit that implementation automatically and need no changes. New classes may override the default to provide specialized behavior. If your default relies on other abstract methods, ensure those methods will behave correctly for existing implementers. Also test the case where a class implements two interfaces that both offer a default with the same signature — the compiler will require the class to override and resolve the conflict. If the method cannot have a sensible default for all implementers, consider creating a new interface or providing a utility class instead. This process keeps libraries usable by older code while allowing the A P I to grow responsibly. Here are the essential ideas to carry forward. First, an interface is a behavioral contract that declares what methods an implementing class must provide; it expresses capability, not state. Second, interfaces enable multiple inheritance of type, allowing classes to implement multiple contracts and be used polymorphically. Third, Java 8 introduced default methods so interfaces can add concrete behavior without breaking existing implementations; this lets APIs evolve safely. Fourth, static methods in interfaces provide utility functions scoped to the interface and must be called on the interface name. Remember the practical design rule: use interfaces for pure behavior contracts, and use abstract classes or composition when you need shared state. Keep interfaces small and focused, prefer defaults only when a safe fallback exists, and explicitly resolve conflicts when multiple defaults collide. These guidelines help you design extensible and maintainable systems where behavior contracts are clear and change can be managed without breaking clients.
